components: The judgment reports that the protected-monuments register identifies the claimant as owner of the particular property. This records the document's reported content without claiming independent inspection or authentication.
The target court records that the manner of the claimant's alleged acquisition of the identified property was not under challenge.
The narrow acquisition-supporting evidentiary conclusion produced by R1 is available for the same claimant and property.
The judgment reports that the relevant city survey records identify the claimant in relation to the disputed property.

A witness is reported to have testified that the claimant possessed the identified property, with supporting testimony about protected-monument status and construction at the claimant government's expense. The proposition establishes the testimony's content, not independently verified possession.

The target court found no concrete evidence on the record substantiating the opponent's competing ownership claim. This is a finding about evidentiary insufficiency, not proof that every historical assertion made by the opponent was false.
The target court found that the claimant did not specifically plead and prove possession excluding the opponent with the intention to possess as owner.
The target court found that the alleged earlier title of the opponent, material to the proposed adverse-possession theory, was not specifically pleaded and proved.

The target court found that the relevant point of time of the supposed dispossession had not been specifically pleaded and proved. This records the missing temporal allegation or proof, not an independently established dispossession event or date.
The claimant asserts ownership originating from an asserted title-acquisition basis independent of adverse possession. This records the pleaded position rather than accepting its truth.
The same claimant asserts adverse possession as an alternative source of ownership of the same property against the identified opponent.

The intermediate conclusion from R3 identifies judicially recorded failures of specific pleading and proof concerning hostile exclusive possession, earlier opposing title and the point of dispossession.
The intermediate conclusion from R4 establishes that the original-title and alternative adverse-possession theories require an inconsistency and renunciation assessment.
The affirmative title evaluation under R2 has independently established the claimant's title on the evidentiary basis being considered, without relying on adverse possession.
The contextual adverse-possession evaluation under R5 has determined that the alternative hostile-possession ground was not established for the same claimant, opponent and property.
Earlier attributed conclusion with all its assumptions retained.
The plaintiff-possessor was judicially found to possess the identified suit property. The proposition concerns possession, not ownership or the precise boundary of the adjoining properties.
The plaintiff failed to establish the claimed title to the suit property. This is a finding of non-proof, not a determination that the plaintiff's ownership claim is factually false.
The independently established possessory basis preserved by R1. This is a derived legal predicate, not a fresh factual finding or an assertion that ownership has been established.

The target court expressly reports that the plaintiff was found to be in settled possession of the identified property. This is accepted as an attributed judicial finding without independently reconstructing every underlying factual attribute.

The purported possessor has only engaged in casual, intermittent, or incomplete acts of intrusion that have not matured into settled possession. Its expected absence in this reconstruction follows from the reported settled-possession classification, not an independently proved chronology of occupation.
The possessory interest protected under R2, based on the requisite settled character of possession and without relying on confirmation of ownership.

The opposing party interfered with or obstructed the possessor's enjoyment of the identified property while asserting a competing ownership claim. In the supplied case, the target court recounts obstruction of the plaintiff's construction on the disputed land; the allegation of ownership remains distinct from proof of ownership.
The possessory basis supplied by R3, which does not require a judicial confirmation of the plaintiff's ownership.

The defendant-appellant's counsel argued that the suit was defective because no declaration of title had been sought despite the title dispute, and that failure to prove title required dismissal notwithstanding established possession. TRUE records that these arguments were made, without accepting their legal correctness or independently verifying every procedural allegation.
The legally independent possessory basis for an injunction established through R3, attached to the identified possessor, opposing claimant, and suit property.
The non-entailment established through R5: protective possessory relief does not itself determine ownership.

The target court reports that the lower courts proceeded on possession without deciding title, and expressly clarifies that the impugned judgment does not determine the suit property's title for or against either litigant. This is a reported judicial reservation, not a substantive finding establishing either party's ownership.

The defendant was also found not to have established title to the disputed land sufficient to substantiate his claimed entitlement to evict the plaintiff. This records failure of proof, not a definitive finding that the defendant lacks any title.
